original_value: Objective: The current research shows the advantage of single-word messages in the particular case of variable message signs (VMSs) with a high aspect ratio. Background: Early studies on traffic sign design proposed that pictorial information would advantage equivalent text messages in static signs. Method: We used a driving simulator to present individually 36 VMSs, showing six words (e.g., “congestion”) and six danger signs (e.g., congestion traffic sign). In Experiment 1, 18 drivers read aloud the text or orally identified the pictograms as soon as they could correctly do it. In Experiment 2, a different sample of 18 drivers gave a motor response, according to the meaning of the message. We analyzed the legibility distance and accuracy, driving performance (speed variability), and glance behavior. Results: Our results show that single-word messages were associated with better performance (farther reading distances) and required less visual demands (fewer glances and less glancing times) than pictograms. Conclusion: As typical configurations of VMSs usually have a high aspect ratio, and thus allow large character heights, single-word messages can outperform the legibility of pictograms. However, the final advantage of text or pictorial messages would depend on several factors, such as the driver’s knowledge of the language and the pictogram set, the use of single or multiple words, the particular design and size of critical details in letters and pictograms, environmental factors, and driver age. Application: Potential applications include the design of VMSs and other devices aimed at displaying text and/or pictograms with a high aspect ratio.

result.paraphrase: Objective: This study indicates that, for variable message signs (VMSs) with a high aspect ratio, single-word messages have an advantage. Background: Earlier work on traffic sign design suggested that pictorial information would have an edge over equivalent text on static signs. Method: We used a driving simulator to show 36 VMSs one by one, including six words (e.g., “congestion”) and six danger signs (e.g., congestion traffic sign). In Experiment 1, 18 drivers read the text aloud or verbally identified the pictograms as quickly as they could do so correctly. In Experiment 2, another group of 18 drivers made a motor response based on the meaning of the message. We assessed legibility distance and accuracy, driving performance (speed variability), and glance behavior. Results: Single-word messages produced better performance, with greater reading distances, and demanded less visual attention, with fewer and shorter glances, than pictograms. Conclusion: Because VMSs typically have a high aspect ratio and therefore permit large character heights, single-word messages can be more legible than pictograms. However, the ultimate advantage of text or pictorial messages depends on several factors, including the driver’s knowledge of the language and pictogram set, whether the message uses one word or multiple words, the specific design and size of critical details in letters and pictograms, environmental conditions, and driver age. Application: Potential uses include designing VMSs and other devices intended to display text and/or pictograms with a high aspect ratio.
